body:
Windows and Linux, both built from `main` at `f9db4ff`.

## The big ones

**Blink replaces the dash.** It goes where you are *aiming*, not where you are walking — so it is a dodge upward out of a shot, a drop through a floor, and a gap-crosser at once. Three ticks of no collision and total immunity, with a shrink-to-a-sliver animation and a new, much quieter sound.

**One consequence worth knowing before you play:** because it follows aim, you cannot retreat with it unless you turn around — and turning around means not shooting. The dash was an escape; this is a commitment.

**The arena is light-painted neon.** Dark geometry with lit silhouette edges, per-stage palettes swept across the arena (cool at one end, hot at the other), player identity halos, additive bullet cores and trails.

**The card pick is rebuilt** as dark polished slabs with a hairline edge in the card's own colour, TextMeshPro letters with a real bevel, and a colour code derived from what each card actually does — green movement, red offence, copper protection, violet control. The same ink appears on the corner legend.

## Also in this build

- **Camera frames the fight** now, with a punch-in and slow motion on a kill
- **Yeeeuge** actually makes you bigger, 1.25x a copy, capped at 10x
- **Slipstream** can finally be ridden — its recoil now clears walk speed, and the haste that was raising its own threshold is gone
- **Joining defaults to `shoosting.advancedstudios.net`**, with F2 to reset the address
- Explosions respect shields and fire `OnKill` / `OnTakeDamage` — Grenadier, Mayhem, Radiance, Executioner and Brawler all behave differently now
- Fall kills are credited to whoever knocked you off
- Card picks time out after 20s instead of stalling the lobby
- Relay drops peers that are talking but not advancing, so a stalled client can no longer hold a lobby for hours

## Not verified

How any of the feel changes land — the camera, the blink window and cooldown, and whether Slipstream is rideable in practice. That is what this build is for.

181 headless tests pass on Linux, Windows and macOS.
name: dev build - neon art pass, blink, and five fixes

body:
Windows and Linux from `main` at `e7c943d`. The LAN relay is already running this code.

## The join screen actually works now

The lobby size could not be changed from that screen at all, and adding 3 to the range did not fix it because the range was never the problem: entering the screen focused the address field and nothing ever unfocused it. The settings keys are guarded against firing while you type - an address is mostly digits - so with the field permanently focused, every one of those keys went into the hostname. Players, length, stage and delay were all unreachable, not just the size.

**TAB** now switches between the address and the settings, and the screen opens on the settings. Set the lobby with `2` / `3` / `4`, arrows for length and stage, and press enter without touching the address.

Only the **first player in** needs to set any of this. Slot zero broadcasts the whole lobby config and everyone else adopts it, so a joiner needs an address and nothing else.

## Also in this build

**Cards are no longer taken before you see them.** Taking a card is a one second hold, and the hold refuses to start until the confirm has been released since the screen opened - so a button held from the fight counts for nothing.

**Everyone watches the pick**: the description shows immediately rather than only after the picker moves, and the hold bar is broadcast so the lobby watches it fill.

**A mistimed block kills you.** A shot that reached you before the shield came up used to be trapped in the bubble costing nothing; every pass now deals its damage. A block made in time is still free. Window 0.30s, cooldown 1.8s.

**The relay drops peers that talk without playing**, so a stalled client can no longer hold a lobby.

## Known and not fixed

The join panel's lines overlap each other at higher resolutions. Ugly, blocks nothing, and has its own pass coming.

## Not verified

The hold bar has not been seen from this end - the bot fixture picks instantly, so every capture landed on a fight. Nor have the block numbers been played.

body:
Overnight session. Three things landed, and five issues closed that turned out to be already built.

## This build can update itself

`update.cmd` now ships next to `shoosting.exe` — double-click it and it fetches the newest release, keeps the build you were on in `previous_version_1` (three deep), installs the new one, and asks whether to launch. `update.sh` does the same on Linux.

**This only works forward.** Your current install has no updater in it, so this one has to be unzipped by hand once. Every build after it updates itself.

It needs a credential, because the repo is private: it uses the GitHub CLI's login if you have one (you do, on the Windows box), otherwise a token in `github-token.txt` beside the script.

## Cards say what they are

Every card now carries keywords, and the first one is its primary — which is what paints its tile. Sixteen cards change colour, all of them from "whichever stat bucket its effects happened to fall in" to a declared identity. Venom is a poison card now, not a bullet-stats card.

The pool hash covers keywords, so `LobbyConfig.Version` went 6 -> 7. **Everyone in a lobby needs this build.**

## The announcer's script is a data file

All 199 written and 134 spoken lines moved out of C# into `script.json`. No lines changed — verified byte-for-byte — and no audio was re-baked. It is groundwork for player-submitted shit-talking (#72): a proposed line is now a one-line diff instead of C# a bot would have to write.

## Closed as already done

#22 (relay command reliability), #38 (card pick timer), #47 (Slipstream), #34 (match camera), #9 (visual identity). Each has a comment naming the code that proves it. Every remaining open issue was audited and the partly-done ones now say precisely which half exists.

## Verified

247 headless tests on Linux, Windows and macOS; a two-peer relay match where neither peer ever pressed a key held identical checksums for 99 SYNC ticks; the updater run end to end against the real release including four forced installs capping at `previous_version_3`; and a running player rendering an announcer line out of the new data file.

**Not verified:** `update.sh` has never executed — no Linux box here. Impact damage tuning is still unplayed.
name: dev build - it updates itself now, and cards say what they are

body:
Windows and Linux from `main` at `a868fa3`. Fixes the regression in the previous build.

## What was broken

After a three-player round dealt both cards, the round stopped restarting and nobody respawned.

Closing a pick does two things: it ends the pick, and it restores the phase the round decided - which the open had stashed away so the world could keep running underneath the pick screen. Restoring consumes it. The match layer was closing after *every* pick, which was correct when there was only ever one; with two picks the first one spent the phase, the second re-captured the wrong one, and the final close restored something that meant nothing.

Now only the last pick of a round closes it. The ones before it hand over, which resets the screen for the next player and restarts their expiry clock - without that, the second picker inherits the first one's deadline, which after a slow first pick has often already passed, and their card gets chosen for them the moment it appears.

## About the desync

The headless three-peer test that reproduces this shows the peers **staying in agreement** - what breaks is the round never restarting. So what looked like a desync was most likely the stall: everybody frozen, nobody respawning, on every machine at once.

If a genuine `SYNC tick=... checksum=...` mismatch shows up in a client log, that is a separate bug and this build does not fix it. Worth keeping an eye out.

## New coverage

Three-peer round-flow tests, because a duel has one loser and therefore never hands the pick over - every part of this was invisible below three players, and the existing two-peer coverage passed throughout.

194 headless tests pass on Linux, Windows and macOS.
name: dev build - the round restarts again after both picks

body:
Windows and Linux from `main` at `a14566e`. The LAN relay is already current.

## The three-player card pick is fixed

Two bugs, both invisible in a duel and both live the moment a third player joined.

**Only one loser was offered a card.** A three-player round has one winner and two losers, and only one of them got a pick - so the other was punished twice for the same round: they lost it, then watched somebody else collect the compensation for losing it. Everybody who did not win now owes a pick, taken in turn, so a three-player round runs two picks back to back and a four-player round runs three.

**The same player picked almost every round.** The choice of which loser used a strict less-than over slot order, so whenever the scores were level - every opening round, and most rounds of a close match - the lowest-numbered loser always won the tie. In a duel that is invisible because there is only ever one loser. With three players it meant the host picked nearly every round regardless of who had won.

Ties are now drawn by lot inside the simulation, so every peer resolves them the same way. Hand size breaks the tie first: a player holding fewer cards is behind in a way the round score does not show. Whoever is furthest behind still gets first refusal - the lot only ever settles a genuine tie.

## Not verified

How a three-player round feels with two picks running back to back. It may want a beat between them.

Also still unplayed from this end: the card hold bar, and the mistimed-block numbers.

189 headless tests pass on Linux, Windows and macOS.

body:
Everyone needs this build: **the protocol byte moved to 6**, so an older peer is refused rather than desyncing.

## Walls, floors and ceilings hurt

Terrain used to be scenery. You could be flung the length of the arena into a wall and arrive unharmed. Now a surface charges for the speed you meet it with.

- Ordinary movement is free. Running into a wall and landing off a jump cost nothing, deliberately.
- **Sliding along a wall is free; arriving at one is not.** Only speed heading *into* a surface counts.
- Getting flung out of the arena hard now costs a lot more than drifting out of it.
- **Shooting somebody into a wall is a kill you get credited for.**
- A live block saves you outright.

Rough shape: a full-height fall costs about twelve, terminal velocity about thirty, and a blast that flings somebody across the arena can be nearly lethal on its own.

**This is the part that needs your eyes.** The threshold is set at 36 and I cannot tell you whether that is right — say if hard falls chip you too often, or if being launched still feels survivable when it shouldn't. It is a one-line change either way.

## Card picking shows the numbers

The pick screen showed a card's prose and nothing else, which meant the numbers were missing at the one moment they decide something. It now shows the same breakdown the hand hover does — worked out against the hand you are holding, **including the copy you are about to take**. So a fifth Yeeeuge says what five would actually do, not what one does.

## Verified

221 headless tests pass on Linux, Windows and macOS, including the golden checksum, which was regenerated deliberately for the new damage source. Unity compiles clean. The pick screen layout was checked on screen against a four-effect card.

**Not verified:** how any of it feels. No two real peers have been on the relay with this build either.
name: dev build - walls hurt now, and cards show their numbers

body:
Everyone needs this build: **the protocol byte moved to 5**, so a peer on an older build is refused rather than desyncing.

## What changed

The lobby's card configuration was a 64-bit mask indexed by each card's *position* in the library. That capped the game at 64 cards with 59 written, and inserting or removing a card silently changed what an existing selection meant.

That is gone. A match now holds a card pool, and a card that is not in the pool is not in the match — so the ceiling does not exist any more rather than having been raised.

The wire carries the set selection plus a hash of the pool it builds. If two builds would play with different cards, the join is refused up front instead of the match quietly coming apart minutes later.

## What to look for

Nothing should feel different. Card offers *are* different — the pool is now sorted by id, which changes what any given seed deals — but the distribution and the set toggles behave as before.

Worth a look:
- card sets on and off from the setup menu, and the count it reports
- a three-player online round, since the pick queue is where card changes surface
- `-cards core,chaos` on the command line still filters

## Verified

210 headless tests pass on Linux, Windows and macOS, including the golden checksum, which was regenerated deliberately for the new pool order. Unity compiles clean and the player runs for 40 seconds with bots and no exceptions.

**Not verified:** nothing was played by hand, and no two real peers were put on the relay — the join-refusal path has only been tested in-process.
name: dev build - card pool replaces the 64-card mask

body:
Windows and Linux from `main` at `4df3318`.

## Point at any card to read it

The corner grids have shown every hand all match as two-letter codes, which tells you how far somebody has escalated and nothing about what any of it does. Hover one - anybody's, including while you are dead and waiting - and it says what the card is.

**With the stack worked out.** Most of this game compounds: two Bullet Times is 1.6 squared, not 3.2, so five cards deep nobody can tell how much of their build is one card. A hovered card shows the per-copy effect and, if they hold more than one, what the pile comes to - `+60% each -> +156% with 2`.

Cards that do several things get a line each, so Yeeeuge reports its health and its size separately - they compound independently. Triggered effects are named rather than summed, because two copies of a shield-on-hit shield twice and calling that "200%" would be a lie.

## The shield, again

Window 0.45s, cooldown 0.88s - available about half the time now. A mistimed block is lethal, so the risk lives in the timing rather than in the recovery. Blocking also throws an airblast: a ring that leaves the body and thins as it goes, separate from the shield itself because they say different things.

## Gecko is gone

Agreed as a group. Removing a card changes the size and rarity mix of the pool, which changes the draw sequence for the whole match - so this is a bigger change than it looks, and deliberate.

## The pick feed moved

It was a grey box in the top right sitting over the arena for twelve seconds. Now it is under the score, with no panel behind it, gone in four.

## Not verified

The moved pick feed has not been seen in place from this end, and the stack arithmetic has only been read at one copy - the compounding line wants somebody holding three of something.

body:
Windows and Linux, both from `main` at `40cf32d`.

## What is new since dev-f9db4ff

**A mistimed block now kills you.** A shot that reached your body before the shield came up used to be trapped inside the bubble - reversing every tick, doing nothing, costing nothing. Blocking late was indistinguishable from blocking well. Every pass through the body now deals the shot's damage, credited to whoever fired it, so a trapped round finishes the job.

A block made in time is untouched: the punish only triggers when the shot is already *inside* you, which only happens when the shield arrives after the round does.

**The shield timing changed to match.** The old numbers were a 0.22s read punished by five seconds of nothing - about a 4% duty cycle, so whether a shot arrived while your block was live was mostly luck. Now that a bad block hurts, the risk lives in the timing:

| | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| Window | 0.22s | 0.30s |
| Cooldown | 5.0s | 1.8s |

Blocking should now be something you do often and can get wrong, rather than a lottery ticket.

## Still in from the previous build

The blink, the neon arena, the rebuilt card pick, the framing camera, Yeeeuge, Slipstream, the relay liveness fix and the explosion damage path. See dev-f9db4ff for those notes.

## Relay note

The relay fix from the last build only takes effect once the relay itself is redeployed - the copy running on the LAN is older than this. Clients do not need it to play; it only affects a stalled peer holding a lobby.

## Not verified

Whether 0.30s and 1.8s are the right numbers. They are reasoned from the duty cycle, not played - that is the main thing this build is for.

body:
**Thruster is a real thruster now.** This is the one to play.

## Thruster

A landed shot **sticks to whatever it hit and keeps pushing** for a second and a half, in the direction the bullet was travelling. It does not re-aim.

- **It lasts.** Knockback happens and is over; this is still working a second later. That is the whole difference between the old card and this one.
- **It stacks.** Every hit adds to the push, so landing a burst genuinely moves somebody — a couple of hits will carry a player off a ledge they would have survived.
- **You get the credit.** A push that takes somebody off the map is your kill even if the shot was five seconds ago, which is exactly when this card is most lethal.

Capped at five hits' worth of force — above gravity, so a stack can lift someone, but a whole magazine cannot produce a number with no ceiling.

The old card was a flat knockback multiplier, which is indistinguishable from a slightly stronger gun. That is gone.

**Completely unplayed.** Force, burn length, the cap, and whether a pushed target should still be able to fight the push with normal movement are all things only a controller can answer. Everything is a one-line change.

## Also in here

- **The card offer panel no longer draws through its own footer.** Two bugs: the `holding 2 of these` line cost two rendered lines, and Sniper has five effects and had been colliding since effect lines existed. Both fixed, and it is a test now rather than a note asking someone to check it on screen.
- **An MCP server** that hosts the simulation itself — no Unity, no running game. It can list and describe cards, compile a build's stats, and run headless matches. Groundwork for #24.
- **The announcer script round-trip**, so edits made in the editor page can be merged back into the game with validation instead of by hand.

## Worth knowing

**Blink may be self-harming.** A blink moves at 90 units/sec and the impact rule charges most of a health bar for arriving at a wall that fast — a bot found this by killing itself on the opening tick. Wall-clinging is exempt from impact damage; blink is not. If dashing into a wall feels punishing, that is why, and it is a two-line fix once you have an opinion.

**The Linux zip is missing from this release on purpose.** The Linux player segfaults on launch and every previous release shipped it broken — see #80. Shipping nothing is more honest than shipping that.

## Verified

297 headless tests on Linux, Windows and macOS. Four sabotages of the thruster logic, all caught by tests. Unity compiles clean, and the build runs a headless bot match with zero exceptions. The test suite also now passes natively on the Linux box, not only in CI.
name: dev build - Thruster actually thrusts

## What changed

**Cards are no longer taken before you see them.** The pick screen opens the instant a round ends, and if you were firing - most rounds - you were still holding the button on that frame, so a press committed immediately and took whatever happened to be highlighted.

Taking a card is now a one second hold. The part that actually fixes it is the arming rather than the duration: the hold refuses to start until the confirm has been *released* since the screen opened, so a button already down when the round ends counts for nothing.

**The relay drops peers that talk without playing.** A stalled client used to hold a lobby against every join indefinitely, because silence was the only liveness test and a stuck lockstep peer keeps sending keepalives. It now watches whether the tick advances. This is live on the LAN relay as of this build.

Hover stopped being retransmitted - it is superseded by the next one, so repeating a lost one delivers something already stale. The card pick itself still retransmits, because losing *that* is what strands a lobby.

The hold bar has not been seen on screen from this end - the bot fixture picks instantly, so every capture landed on a fight instead. It is simple UI and compiles clean, but you will see it before I do.

Second build of the night. Everything in `dev-afd9fa1` plus the desync alarm — **update to this one**, the previous release's protocol byte is already stale.

## Desyncs report themselves now

The checksum has been logged every sixty ticks for a long time and nothing looked at it: finding a desync meant running two peers, keeping both logs and joining them by hand — which only works if you already suspected one.

Peers now exchange the number and compare it. The first tick where two worlds differ names itself, on the machine it happened on, as `DESYNC tick=... peer=... ours=... theirs=...`.

It reports rather than halting. Halting on a false positive would be worse than the status quo, and nothing has seen this fire in anger yet.

`LobbyConfig.Version` 7 -> 8. **Everyone in a lobby needs this build.** If you already have `dev-afd9fa1`, `update.cmd` will fetch it.

## Everything from dev-afd9fa1

- **This build updates itself.** `update.cmd` next to `shoosting.exe` fetches the newest release, keeps the last three builds in `previous_version_1..3`, and asks whether to launch.
- **Cards say what they are.** Every card carries keywords; the primary paints its tile. Sixteen cards change colour.
- **The announcer's script is a data file** — groundwork for player-submitted lines (#72).
- Five issues closed as already built, and every remaining open issue audited.

## Verified

258 headless tests on all three platforms. A ninety-second two-peer match through the real relay: 88 checksum exchanges each, zero alarms, zero exceptions — so the alarm is silent when it should be. Three sabotages of the alarm, all caught by tests, including the sign-extension bug that would have made half of all checksums read as a desync.

**Not verified:** `update.sh` still has never executed. Impact damage tuning is still unplayed.
name: dev build - desyncs report themselves

body:
Two changes, both on branch `relay-stale-peer-tick`.

## The relay lockout

The relay claiming to be "full" with nobody connected was the client's own refusal, not the relay's. `RelayClient.HighestPeerTick` was a permanent high-water mark: the join screen reads it to ask *"is a match under way?"* but what it answered was *"did a match ever run?"* Watch one match from the join screen and every later lobby, empty relay included, is refused with MATCH ALREADY IN PROGRESS until you relaunch. `ForgetSlot` — the recovery path for a restarted relay — cleared everything except this, so the mechanism meant to heal it preserved the cause.

It is now evidence of *now*: stamped when raised, expired after 3s without confirmation, dropped with the slot it belonged to.

## Lobby size 2-4 from the menu

The join screen's player count was a 2-or-4 toggle — digit `1` gave two, digit `2` gave four, and 3 was unreachable from the menu despite `-players 3` always having worked. The digit is now the count (`2`/`3`/`4`), the pad steps and wraps, and the label shows a filled track. Default unchanged at 2. Track and hints derive from `WorldState.MaxPlayers`, so raising the cap widens the control.

No wire or simulation change, so `LobbyConfig.Version` is unchanged.

## Verified

- Two new `RelayClientPeerTickTests` drive a real client from a fake relay over loopback; both fail against the old code, pass against the new.
- `SessionDeterminismTests` was hardcoded to two peers, so no lobby larger than a duel had ever been run. Size is now threaded through, every peer is compared against the first, and `EveryLobbySizeStaysIdentical` covers 2/3/4 under uneven latency.
- 130 headless tests pass, golden checksum unmoved. Unity compiles clean.

## Not verified

- No runtime test on the build machine: the Linux player segfaults at startup in every mode, including a local `-bots` game that never constructs a `RelayClient`. `si_code` is `SI_USER`, so the signal is sent rather than faulted, and a core with the same signature predates these changes. Separate issue, but it blocked the two-peer check here.
- The join screen itself. No display and no input synthesis, so the track's layout and the pad stepping are unchecked.
- A 3-player lobby is proven in sync headlessly but has never had three real clients on it.

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

https://claude.ai/code/session_01Eidq8PaPFBhYm4H2vctCyW

body:
﻿Fixes the three things mh hit playing over the relay, plus the reset problem behind them.

**The round never restarted after an online card pick.** Online the world keeps running underneath a pick, which meant overwriting the round phase with Intermission - and that threw away the only record of what the round had just decided. RoundOver and MatchOver both became Intermission, which never leaves itself, so when the pick applied there was no next round, no vote, and the player who picked never respawned.

**The card selection was unusable.** The tick loop reset the highlighted card to the first offer sixty times a second, so arrow keys moved the selection and the next tick put it back. The third card could not be reached at all. It was never the mouse wheel.

**Leaving an online match for the main menu left the lobby wiring in place**, so the next local match treated player 2 as a second hotseat player instead of a bot and waited for a vote from someone on another computer.

**A new match now resets everything by construction.** The world is rebuilt rather than tidied, and a test dirties every field by reflection and fails naming anything that survived - which is what stops a card outliving the match it was drawn in.

**The card pick is no longer invisible to everyone else.** Watchers see the same three cards with the picker's highlight moving on them.

**New: `-steamlobby <id>`.** The Steam host logs its lobby id and a second machine can join it directly, without the two accounts needing to be Steam friends first. Untested - no Steam client on the build machine.

Protocol version 3. Both peers and the relay must be on this build.

Linux: `chmod +x shoosting` after unzipping - the archive was made on Windows and does not carry the executable bit.
name: dev build - online card pick fixes, full match reset, shared hover

body:
## You can see your magazine now

Ammo has been in the simulation since the start and nothing ever drew it, so the only way to find out you were empty was to pull the trigger and hear nothing.

A **pip per round** under the health bar, up to ten. A discrete count is what you actually act on — "two left" is a decision, "twenty percent" is not.

Past ten rounds it falls back to a bar. Pips stop being countable at a glance around there, and cards can drive `MagazineSize` to 200 — a quad per round is the exact shape of the mesh-vertex crash this project already hit once with an uncapped pip row.

**Reloading** replaces the readout entirely with a progress sweep in a different colour, filling toward ready. During a reload the interesting number isn't how many rounds you have — it's zero — it's how long until you have any.

It hides on a full magazine that isn't reloading, matching the health bar's rule that the screen stays quiet until something is worth knowing. Say the word if you'd rather it were always on; it is one line.

## Escape always works

It was silently refused during a check-in vote. The stated reason — that pausing a live timed vote would let one player stall the lobby — was already stale: online, a pause is **local**, and the session keeps advancing and delivering everyone's commands underneath it, specifically so one player opening a menu cannot stop the world for anyone else. So the refusal bought nothing and only meant the key was dead on one screen out of ten.

Escape from a vote now pauses and returns you to the vote. The pause menu also had to learn that a check-in, an end vote and a card pick are all still *in a match* — the arena is live under all three and you can be shot during them, so "not in a match" would have been a lie on the very screen where calling a vote is most topical.

## Verified

99 headless tests. Unity compiles clean on both platforms. A four-player bot match ran 30 s with no exceptions.

**Not verified:** how the pip row reads at speed, and whether it sits at the right height above the character. Both are single constants in `PoseAmmo` — tell me which way to nudge them.
name: dev build - magazine readout, Escape always works

body:
## You can see everyone's cards now, permanently

The hover tally is gone. Each corner carries one player's whole hand as a grid of tiles, always on.

Every card has a **two-letter code**, periodic-table style — `Bt` Bullet Time, `Oc` Overcharge, `Gr` Grenadier, `Eh` Event Horizon. Codes rather than names because a hand runs to twenty-four cards and no layout fits that many names and stays readable.

Escalation is the whole shape of a run, and it was unreadable: working out what the player deleting you was holding cost a mouse move and then covered the arena while you read it. "Why am I suddenly losing" should be answerable without taking your hands off the controls.

Details that will matter in play:
- **Corners are fixed by slot** — P1 is always top-left. Your cards never jump corners because somebody else left.
- The grid fills **from the corner outward**, so it grows away from the edge rather than sliding across it as a hand fills.
- Past fifteen cards the last tile becomes a count (`+9`), so a long run reads honestly instead of silently truncating.

## On emoji

I looked into it properly and it does not work here. The HUD is Unity's legacy `Text` against the built-in `LegacyRuntime.ttf`, which has **no emoji glyphs** — they would render as tofu boxes, and any OS fallback would differ between your Windows machine and a Mac. Colour emoji would need TextMeshPro plus a sprite asset, which `Hud.cs` deliberately avoids depending on, and the glyph literals would sit in `CardLibrary.cs` against this project's own no-emoji rule.

**Drawn procedural icons are the real answer** — same approach as `Primitives`, asset-free, renders everywhere. They can replace the codes per card without touching the layout, so it can be done a few cards at a time rather than all sixty at once.

## Also cleaned up

The legend icon row, the hover panel and `HandLegendRows` are gone rather than left sitting unreferenced as a second, worse answer to the same question.

## Verified

100 headless tests. Unity compiles clean on both platforms. Four-player bot match, no exceptions.

**Not verified:** how the grid reads in play, whether fifteen tiles is the right cap, or whether four corner grids crowd the arena. All single constants in `Hud` — `MaxCardTiles`, `CardTileSize`, `CardTileColumns`.
name: dev build - every hand visible in the corners

body:
**Cards stack.** Everything from `dev-05906df` plus two draw rules that were wrong.

## Stacking

`CardDraw.Offer` refused any card already in your hand, so a build could only ever be *widened*, never deepened. That is backwards for this game — `CardCompiler` already applies every copy in a hand, so a second Bullet Time multiplies on top of the first (1.6 x 1.6 = 2.56x). The draw was the only thing standing in the way.

You now get the choice between doubling down on what you have and branching into something new, which is the decision the escalation was built for.

An offer still never repeats a card **within itself** — three identical choices is not a choice.

## Executioner is out of duels

Anything that pays out on a kill is worthless when a kill ends the round: the heal lands in an intermission with nobody left to spend the advantage on. It was wasting the losing player's pick at the exact moment they most needed a real one.

`CardData` gains `MinPlayers` (default 2); Executioner declares 3. A general mechanism rather than a special case, because anything else keyed on `OnKill` deserves the same treatment and a hardcoded id would have to be rediscovered every time.

## Also in this build, from the overnight merges

Drops and rejoins apply on their agreed tick. Match configuration — cards, stage, extend length — is declared in one place. The desync checksum now watches every player timer, all status magnitudes, and four projectile fields it was walking past. Broadphase queries are 3.9x faster and no longer drop a collision candidate at cell boundaries. Plus 35 trash-talk announcer lines.

**Both peers must pass matching `-players`, `-bestof`, `-stage`, `-cards` and `-extend`.** A mismatch is now visible in both logs but is still not refused.

## Verified

99 headless tests. Unity compiles clean, both platforms. A four-player bot match ran 30 s with no exceptions. Two peers over a relay on this exact build: **29 shared SYNC checksums, all agreeing**.

Not verified: how stacked builds actually feel. Two copies of Overcharge is 3.24x damage with 6.76x recoil, and nobody has played that yet — it may be brilliant or it may be unplayable. That is the thing to go and find out.
name: dev build - cards stack now

body:
**The announcer has a voice, and the two things you hit in the last build are fixed.**

## Fixed

**The vote no longer asks a bot to vote.** The screen advertised `P2 R-Alt / R-Ctrl` whenever the lobby had more than one slot, whether or not player 2 was a bot. Nothing was truly blocked — bots vote for themselves — but the screen was telling you to press keys for a player who was never going to press them. It also let the person at the keyboard cast both votes and decide the match twice.

**Enter starts a new match after conceding.** Conceding removes a player, and the new-match reset cleared scores, hands, rounds and cards but never brought anyone back. The match then started with one player present, `StartNextRound`'s "a round needs somebody in it" guard fired, and it bounced straight back to the result screen. `ResetRound` *does* restore presence on round zero, which is why this looked like it should already work — but the guard runs before it.

## The announcer speaks

Formant speech synthesis, generated at runtime. No assets, no licence, no download.

**It approximates speech rather than pronouncing it.** Letters map to phonemes by rule and English spelling defeats that, so expect the rhythm and roughly the vowels to land, not a transcript. Three formants over a sawtooth for voiced sounds, noise for fricatives, a gap and a burst for plosives. Excitement raises the pitch and shortens the delivery, so a triple kill is not read in the same tone as a round starting.

Real neural TTS via Piper is filed as ADV-85. That is the route to something a stranger could understand.

**I have no audio device on this machine.** Every value in the voice — formant positions, phoneme lengths, pitch range, saturation — was chosen from theory and has never been heard by anyone. Assume the first listen is rough.

One bug did get caught by arithmetic rather than by ear: the resonator is only stable while `2*pi*hz/rate` stays under one, which caps out near 3.9 kHz at this sample rate, and the fricative shapes were asking for 6.2. It would have gone divergent and then been normalised into something loud rather than something obviously broken. Formants are clamped now.

## Also in this build

Everything from `dev-511fd04`: the compact card picker, the pick feed showing what everyone took, three stages, twelve cards, impact sparks, the aimed bottom bounce, and the two online desync fixes.

## Verified

88 headless tests pass. Unity compiles clean. A headless bot match ran forty-five seconds through rounds and a result with no exceptions.

Not verified: how any of it looks or sounds.
name: dev build - announcer speaks, bot vote and concede loop fixed

body:
**The pit was inescapable by arithmetic, not by feel. Fixed.**

## The pit

The boundary was a fixed 30 by 22 on every stage, while the camera can only see about ten units down. Falling put you near y −20, and the bounce threw you up 6.5 units — `v²/2g` at a flat launch of 26 — reaching y −14 with the lowest platform at −6. **No input could close that gap.** You bounced until the 25-per-bounce charge killed you.

Two changes:

**The boundary now follows the stage's view** — the visible frame plus 40% of its half-extent on every side. Falling off the screen is answered while you are still near the stage, on every stage, with no per-stage table to keep correct.

**The bottom launch is solved, not fixed.** It takes whatever vertical speed reaches the middle of the arena, plus a little overshoot so you arrive with something left rather than stalling at the apex. Checked against all nine stages — each now clears its own lowest platform with room.

**All four edges aim at the centre now.** The sides used to push straight inward and the ceiling straight down, so leaving near a corner put you back beside the corner you left. One rule for the whole boundary.

## The announcer voice is off by default

It was bad. You were right. `-voice` turns it back on if you want it; otherwise the announcer is silent text again, as it was.

Not deleted, because the code is fine and only the sound is not — and it is a reasonable fallback if real voice lines ever fail to load. Real neural TTS via Piper is ADV-85. I am not going to blind-tune a voice on a machine with no audio device; that is what produced the last one.

## Also fixed

The vote no longer advertises `P2 R-Alt / R-Ctrl` when player 2 is a bot, and Enter starts a new match after conceding instead of looping back to the result screen.

## Verified

89 headless tests pass. The golden checksum is untouched. Unity compiles clean. A headless bot match ran forty seconds with no exceptions. Every stage's escape height was checked as arithmetic rather than opinion.

Not verified: whether the new boundary distance feels right to play against. That is the number most likely to want moving, and it is one constant.
name: dev build - the pit is escapable, announcer voice off by default

body:
**The card pick is readable now, and two desyncs that would have ruined online play are gone.**

## What to look at first

**The card picker is no longer full-screen.** A modal scrim is right for a pause menu, where nothing is happening behind it, and wrong for a card pick — online the world keeps running underneath, so blacking it out hid a fight you were still in and could still be killed in.

**You can see what everyone else took.** A pick is the most consequential thing that happens between rounds and it used to be invisible: you saw "PLAYER 2 IS PICKING", then nothing, and next round you were being deleted faster with no way to know why.

I have no display on the build machine, so **the proportions of both are reasoned rather than seen**. Panel size, position and the feed's placement are the values most likely to be wrong. They are single constants and quick to change.

## Two desyncs fixed

**The card pick restarted the round off-tick, and skipped the picker entirely.** `DrawCardPick` runs from the frame path, and its `ClosePick` went on to reset the round — the view layer writing to the world at frame rate. Worse, the picker left the pick screen the moment it broadcast, so it never ran that code at all. Everyone else restarted the round and the picker did not. That is exactly the "player 2 didn't respawn, then player 1 slid off the left edge" report.

**Online play never declared the match rules.** The join path set neither `WinsNeeded` nor the check-in round, so a peer joining with `-skipmenu` kept menu defaults while the host had chosen something else. They then disagreed about when the match ends and when a check-in falls due — both of which write to the world. Match length is now declared with `-bestof`, on the same footing as `-players`.

**Both machines must pass the same `-players` and `-bestof`.**

## Content

Three stages. **THE SPIRE** inverts THE PIT — the height is in the middle, so the strong position is the exposed one. **CATHEDRAL** puts columns squarely in the firing lane, which makes it the home stage for Bouncy and Grenadier. **THE MAW** hangs teeth from the roof as well as the floor, so every route is a gap to fit through.

Twelve cards across gunplay, movement, defence and chaos. Sniper, Flak, Heavy Rounds, Homewrecker, Sprinter, Anvil, Slipstream, Second Wind, Bulwark, Thornmail, Swarm, Event Horizon. Every one carries a real cost.

## Feel

Impacts now draw where they happen — sparks styled by what landed, with terrain hits shown for the first time. Explosions draw their ring at the blast radius the event actually carries. Bullets flare as they leave the barrel.

Falling out of the bottom now throws you back toward the middle, aimed rather than straight up. The old behaviour dropped you through very nearly the same hole, so leaving near a corner meant bouncing at the corner.

The arena boundary has a sound for the first time. **Never played on the build machine — there is no audio device here.** Judge it and tell me.

## Netcode

The relay now reports every peer's tick, packet rate and silence, and calls out peers that have drifted apart. It is the only place that sees both clocks at once.

Lockstep now runs over any link, and the Steam path exists: lobby, mesh, session. **None of the Steam code has ever executed** — no client, no App ID past Spacewar on this machine.

A two-peer test found a real race: the first `SubmitLocal` overwrote the session's reserved empty opening ticks with real input and transmitted it, so which version a peer used came down to packet timing. On a LAN the real input almost always won on both machines, which is why it never showed up here and would have on a real connection.

## Verified

88 headless tests pass. Two peers played over the relay for roughly two thousand ticks with every shared checksum matching. No exceptions in either log.

Not verified: how any of it looks or sounds, and every line of the Steam path.
name: dev build - card picker, pick feed, three stages, twelve cards

body:
**Five branches merged overnight.** All reviewed, all verified together before merging.

## Netcode correctness

**Drops and rejoins now apply on their agreed tick.** `PeerDropped` used to fire the moment the notice arrived, and the handler calls `RemovePlayer` — which mutates the world and can cascade into a card pick, which *draws from the shared random stream*. Two peers doing that on different ticks is a desync. Also fixes `AdmitPeer`, which readmitted a returning player immediately and would have stalled the session forever on the ticks before their agreed return.

**Match configuration is declared in one place.** Card pool, stage and extend length were never agreed between peers. A different card pool is the nastiest: `CardDraw.Offer` rejects different indices on each machine and consumes a *different number of random draws*, so the streams diverge permanently and never recover. There is now one struct, one reader, one writer — a setting added to it cannot reach a match unapplied, which is the property the previous two fixes of this same bug lacked.

New flags: `-cards`, `-extend`, and `-stage` now reaches the online path. **Both peers must still pass matching flags** — a mismatch is now visible in both logs but is not yet refused.

**The desync alarm was ignoring most of the world.** The checksum omitted every player timer, all status magnitudes, `JumpsUsed`/`DashesUsed`, and a projectile's lifetime, damage, remaining bounces and armed flag. A divergence in any of those went unnoticed until it surfaced as a position difference seconds later. Several of this week's bugs would have announced themselves at the tick they happened.

## Performance

**Broadphase queries are 3.9x faster** — 139 ns to 36 ns, measured over 200k queries. `Fix64` division is a software bit loop, and the collision query was spending ~98 ns of it to return under one candidate polygon on average.

It also fixes a real latent bug: rounding could push a box's low edge past a cell it genuinely overlaps, dropping a collision candidate. A projectile could pass through a polygon at a cell boundary.

## Content

**35 new announcer lines** with a trash-talk register, spread across all 16 categories rather than piled into one — the category decides how often a line is heard, so dumping them all in "kill" would have crowded out the existing good ones. No existing line was touched.

## Verified

97 headless tests pass. Unity compiles clean. Two peers played over a relay on this exact build: **31 shared SYNC checksums, all agreeing**, no exceptions, identical config lines in both logs.

Not verified: how the new lines read in play, and the four-player path beyond bots.
name: dev build - five merges: netcode correctness, 3.9x broadphase, trash talk

body:
**Your 480Hz panel was running the simulation eight times too fast.**

Online, one input frame was submitted per *rendered* frame, so the simulation advanced at whatever speed your machine drew at. Ticks are the simulation's clock and they belong to real time — the offline path always knew that and used an accumulator; the online path just didn't.

Two peers drawing at different rates submit at different rates. The session advances at the slowest one while the fastest buffers ahead and saturates its UDP send buffer — which is where **95,000 unhandled exceptions** in a single stalled match came from. Headless with no vsync it hit 54,000 ticks/second and buried the relay under traffic it couldn't forward, which is what made LAN testing look flaky.

Online now uses the same real-time accumulator as offline. While waiting on someone else's input it keeps submitting at the tick rate without advancing, so a peer waiting on you isn't left waiting longer.

## Two supporting fixes
**A full UDP send buffer is not an error** — it's the kernel reporting backpressure, and input is sent redundantly precisely so a lost packet costs nothing. It's tolerated now instead of throwing every frame.

**Joining a match in progress is refused.** Lockstep has no state transfer: a joiner starts at tick 0 while the match is thousands of ticks ahead, and neither side can ever advance again. Joining late didn't degrade the match, it *deadlocked* it. You now get a clear panel, and the lobby heals itself.

## Relay
Needs the update from the previous release (`--players=N` / `SHOOSTING_PLAYERS`). Already redeployed on sunstation.

## Verified
Three consecutive runs against sunstation over the LAN: **1680 ticks in 30 seconds — 28 seconds of game, correctly paced**, identical checksums on every shared tick, zero exceptions. Kill-and-rejoin: the relay returns the slot, the joiner is refused cleanly, the survivor keeps playing. 72 sim tests pass.

**Not verified:** how it feels at a real frame rate on the 480Hz machine — which is the thing this most changes. That one is yours to judge.
name: dev build - online ran at the frame rate

body:
No more command-line switches to play.

## Front end
**Title → Play / Join a game / Settings / Quit.**

**Settings** covers announcer chattiness, volume, bot difficulty and card sets, and persists between runs.

**Join a game** takes a typed relay address and remembers it, so your LAN address is entered once rather than every session. Port defaults to 7777.

## The join screen is temporary by design
It sits behind `FeatureFlags.DirectConnect` and is meant to be deleted once Steam lobbies work. Asking a player for an IP address is exactly the friction Steam invites exist to remove — it is here because the Steam path needs an App ID that does not exist yet, and a LAN needs none of that.

## Relay
Running on sunstation, comes back on reboot:
```
192.168.4.196
```

## Also fixed
Escape on the main menu used to open the *pause* menu, leaving "Leave the match" sitting over a screen where there was no match.

`-skipmenu` and `-connect` still work for automation.
name: dev build - main menu and join by address

body:
**The desync was card picking.** It was built before multiplayer and never wired into it.

Your screenshot showed it exactly: one window mid-round, the other stuck on PICK A CARD. Two faults at once — the pick was applied **locally only**, so the picker's hand existed on one machine and not the other, and entering the pick screen **stopped that peer advancing the session** while the other kept stepping.

Picks now travel as scheduled commands, the same mechanism peer drops use: broadcast with the tick they apply to, so every peer applies the same choice on the same tick.

Verified: identical checksums across **38,799 shared ticks** through many card picks.

Also: **player 1 is blue**, and the relay is published as a container image.

## Relay on a server
```
docker run -d --network host --restart unless-stopped \
  ghcr.io/tehrandom2/shoosting-relay:latest
```
`--network host` matters — LAN broadcast discovery cannot cross a bridge network.

## Reminder
Start a **fresh** relay each session. One left running holds its old peers, so new arrivals get slots 2 and 3 instead of 0 and 1:
```
ss -ulpn | grep 7777
pkill -x shoosting-host
```
name: dev build e33677f - desync fixed

body:
Something is watching your match and has opinions about it.

Chattiness is in the pause menu (**Esc**): off / big moments only / normal / running commentary. Off is genuinely silent.

## What it actually says

Real lines from a real bot match, not mock-ups:

> From 23 metres out! Player 1 never saw the shot.
> A clean sweep for Player 2. Player 1 never got going.
> Returned to sender. Player 1 shot themselves via Player 2.
> Player 1 takes the whole thing!

## The interesting part is what it does *not* say

A first pass announced every block. Against a competent opponent that was nine lines out of twenty-three, and it became noise inside one round.

So it scores moments for notability instead of narrating. A block only earns words if the shot **would actually have killed you**. Ordinary kills are quiet; a kill from across the map, out of the air, off a deflection, or into your own face is not. That took a real match from 23 lines to 11 — every one a genuine moment.

## Multiplayer

Every peer says the same thing with **nothing sent over the network**. Template choice is seeded from values everyone already agrees on, so the draw is reproducible everywhere. Verified by diffing the commentary from two independent processes: identical, line for line.

Text only for now. `AnnouncerLine` carries category, priority and intensity, so a voice model drops in later without changing anything upstream.

## Please tell me

Whether it is funny, and whether it talks too much. Both are one-line changes.
name: dev build b2dad20 - the announcer

body:
Four things landed while you were at work.

## Four new stages
**TOWERS** (climbing, long sightlines) · **THE PIT** (fighting out of a bowl) · **BRIDGES** (punishes momentum) · **SCATTER** (no long sightlines, so arcing and bouncing shots earn their place). Six total, `↑`/`↓` on the setup screen.

Every stage is now covered by a test asserting each tier is reachable from the one below, spawns have ground under them, and the camera contains the platforms — the bug the very first arena shipped with.

## Cards look like something now
Projectiles are styled by **what they do**, not which card made them, so combinations compose: explosive rounds glow, bouncy ones get a hard rim, gravity rounds are heavy and dark, fast ones stretch along their velocity. Trails follow the actual path, so a ricochet turns the corner and an arcing shell curves.

Players show their build — a crimson aura for lifesteal, a pale ring for fragility, a trail for speed builds while moving.

**Hover a player icon at the bottom of the screen to see their hand.** That is competitive information: knowing someone runs Glass Cannon changes how you fight them.

## Disconnects no longer hang the match
Previously one dropped player stalled everyone forever. Now the session waits, drops them, and carries on — verified by killing a peer mid-match and confirming identical checksums across all 13,453 ticks both peers reported.

Nobody has *seen* the new visuals; there is no display on the build machine. If the blast glow reads as mud or the speed stretch is too much at Bullet Time speeds, those are one-line fixes.
name: dev build afe0a39 - stages, visuals, and disconnect handling

body:
**The second player to join was a spectator.** Their character was driven by a bot and their keyboard did nothing.

Input sources are built at startup from `-bots`, which defaults to one bot on slot 1 — and online, only your own slot's source is read. So whichever peer got slot 1 could not play. Fixed: your own slot is always local input, on the primary control scheme, whatever slot number you get.

**Also fixed:** each peer was guessing the lobby size from whatever the relay reported when *it* joined, so the first and second arrivals built different worlds and diverged immediately. Size is now declared with `-players N` (default 2, same on every peer) and a mismatch fails loudly at join.

## Very likely what bit you

**A relay left running from an earlier session.** It still holds the old peers, so new arrivals get slots 2 and 3 instead of 0 and 1 and nothing lines up. It has no window, so it is easy to leave running:

```
ss -ulpn | grep 7777      # something already listening?
pkill -x shoosting-host   # stop it
cd Tools/Host && dotnet run -c Release -- --port=7777
```

Verified with a clean relay: slots 0 and 1, both peers locally controlled, identical checksums across 14,870 ticks.
name: dev build 72ffc3c - multiplayer fix

body:
Twelve cards became forty, and cards can now do things other than change numbers.

## Triggered effects

The old system could only modify stats, which covers about a third of what the genre's cards actually do. Effects now fire on **shooting, hitting, blocking, deflecting, killing, taking damage and reloading**.

That unlocks the interesting half of the pool: Scavenger reloads when you land a hit, Shock Wave hurls everyone away when you block, Teleport blinks you where you are looking, Bombs Away scatters a ring of shots, Venom poisons, Dazzle stuns, Bloodlust makes a kill leave you fast and shielded.

Statuses are real now too - slow, poison, haste, and temporary shields that absorb before health and expire silently.

## Card sets

Press **C** on the setup screen. Five sets: Core, Gunplay, Movement, Defence, Chaos.

Sets rather than individual cards because forty checkboxes is a chore people skip. "No chaos this time" is one keypress.

## Try

- **Defence** set only, and fight with block as your main tool.
- **Chaos** on and watch Demonic Pact plus Radiance turn a round into a firework.
- Turn everything off but Core for something closer to the old feel.
name: dev build 712b589 - 40 cards and card sets

body:
Both bugs you hit, same cause: **the check-in vote was local-only.**

## "It would not start until I pressed Alt for player 2"
`ReadVoteInput` read *both* hotseat key pairs on whichever machine it ran. Those pairs exist so two people can vote from one keyboard — online it meant your machine was being asked to cast player 2's vote. Nothing resolved until you pressed a key that was never yours to press.

Online, a machine now votes only for **its own slot**, and the panel shows only the keys you can actually use: **Space** keep going, **L-Shift** call it.

## "Both players disappeared"
The vote was never sent anywhere. Each machine tallied its own votes, resolved a different result, and removed players the other machine still had. The worlds diverged, and one side started a round with nobody in it.

Votes now travel as scheduled commands with the tick they apply to — the same mechanism card picks and peer drops use — so every peer counts the same tally at the same moment.

The deadline was wall-clock too, so two machines with different frame rates reached it at different moments and could resolve differently *even with identical votes*. It now counts simulation ticks.

Also added a guard so a round can never start with fewer than two players present — that is what turned a desync into an empty arena instead of an error.

## Verified
Two peers, 55 seconds of continuous play through many rounds, votes and card picks: **identical checksums across 53,128 shared ticks**, zero exceptions.

Relay is on sunstation at `192.168.4.196` — and **Join a game** in the main menu now takes the address, no command line needed.
name: dev build - vote desync fixed

body:
Follow-up to the vote fix. That one made votes travel over the network; this one fixes **everything else in the round flow that still ran locally, on a frame.** Four bugs, one shape: a decision that changes the world was being made at a moment only one machine agreed on.

## The vote could not resolve at all
The session stopped advancing whenever the screen was not Playing or CardPick. But a vote is *made of* scheduled commands, and commands are delivered by advancing the session — so opening the vote screen **stopped the very mechanism the vote needed to finish.**

The session now keeps running through votes, picks and the pause menu. That is also what a pause has to mean online: one player opening a menu cannot stop the world for everyone else. Input is neutralised behind a menu instead, so navigating the pause menu no longer walks your character off a ledge you cannot see.

## Resolution ran per frame
Both vote screens removed players and started rounds from the *render* path. Two machines do not agree on when a frame ends, so they resolved at different ticks — a divergence even when the votes matched. Both now resolve from the tick loop, on a tick deadline.

## Leaving removed the wrong player
`LeaveMatch` had **slot zero hard-coded** — player 2 leaving removed player 1, and only on their own machine. Conceding is now a command carrying the leaver's own slot.

## Calling an early vote was local-only
The pause menu opened the end-match vote on one machine while everyone else kept playing a match they did not know was being ended. Now the whole lobby votes together.

## Verified
Two peers, 90 seconds of continuous play: **identical checksums across 86,720 shared ticks**, zero exceptions. 72 sim tests pass.

Not verified by hand with two humans — the menu input paths are the part a bot soak cannot reach. That is where to look if something still feels wrong.
name: dev build - round flow desyncs fixed

body:
Your own bullets can now kill you.

A ricochet into your own face costs **full damage**, and your own explosion hurts you instead of being a free rocket jump.

A shot is harmless to you at the muzzle and arms once it is clear of your body, or the instant it bounces — otherwise firing would kill you on the frame you pulled the trigger. Arming on distance rather than a timer means you can also walk into your own slow projectile.

You cannot lifesteal off yourself.

## Worth trying
- Take **Bouncy** and fight in a corner. It changes the card completely.
- Take **Grenadier** and shoot something close. The knockback used to be free.
- **Bouncy + Grenadier** together is now genuinely dangerous to hold.

```
unzip shoosting-linux64.zip -d shoosting && cd shoosting && chmod +x shoosting && ./shoosting
```
name: dev build 2c91ab1 - self-damage

body:
Falling off no longer kills you.

The arena flings you back in on an arc and charges a **flat 25 health**. Flat rather than a percentage, so building into health actually protects you from it instead of the edge staying equally lethal forever.

**Block as you cross and it is free.** The throw still happens, no damage. It has to be timed, which turns the edge into something you play around rather than something that ends rounds.

Air options are refunded on the way back, so you always get a chance to recover with a dash or wall kick.

Bots know about all of it: their caution now scales with what a fall would actually cost them, so a healthy bot will contest ground near the edge while a bot on its last few points still treats it as lethal. They also spend their block on saving themselves at the boundary.

Worth trying: knock a bot off and watch whether it blocks the crossing.
name: dev build 22d8479 - the edge throws you back

body:
You can now see what the connection is doing.

Previously `-connect` gave no on-screen feedback whatsoever. UDP has no handshake, so a relay that is not running looks identical to one that is — the game just waits. If your connection did not succeed, that is exactly what you would have seen: nothing.

**Now:**
```
CONNECTING
192.168.1.42:7777
waiting for the relay to answer...
attempt 12   ·   6s
```

After 8 seconds it gives up on optimism and lists what to check: is the relay running, is the address right, is it the LAN IP rather than localhost, is UDP 7777 open. **Esc** abandons and drops you into local play.

Once connected, a permanent bottom-left readout:
```
ONLINE   ·   player 2 of 2   ·   tick 1840
```
It turns amber and says **waiting for another player** when the session stalls — lockstep waits for everyone, so that is nearly always the explanation when something feels stuck.

Relay reminder — run it on one machine, then point everyone at that machine's **LAN IP**, not localhost:
```
cd Tools/Host && dotnet run -c Release -- --port=7777
./shoosting -connect 192.168.1.42:7777
```
name: dev build 175e514 - connection feedback

body:
The eyes track the nearest living opponent.

Pupils ease toward their target rather than snapping, so a fast opponent crossing the screen produces a glance instead of a twitch.

They follow the nearest threat rather than whoever you are aiming at — eyes are about awareness, not intent, which will matter more once lobbies are bigger than two.

The body art had the eyes painted on as fixed dots, so the mask is now rasterised without them and the eyes are real sprites that move.
name: dev build 1135587 - they're watching you

body:
**Two machines can play each other.** No Steam, no port forwarding on a LAN, nothing to buy.

## Setup

**One machine runs the relay** (it can also play):
```
cd Tools/Host
dotnet run -c Release -- --port=7777
```
Find that machine's LAN address (`ip addr` / `ipconfig`) — something like `192.168.1.42`.

**Everyone connects**, including on the relay machine:
```
./shoosting -connect 192.168.1.42:7777 -skipmenu
shoosting.exe -connect 192.168.1.42:7777 -skipmenu
```

Slots go in join order, so first to connect is player 1.

## Important

There is **no lobby handshake yet**, so everyone must launch with the same flags — same stage, same settings — or the peers diverge immediately.

Each peer logs a world checksum every second:
```
SYNC tick=180 checksum=0xcfb7a5a9ba745edd
```
**Those must match on every machine.** If they diverge you are playing two different games, and I want to know about it.

## How it works

Peers exchange only their own 6-byte input frames — nothing about the world is ever sent. Because the simulation is deterministic fixed-point, everyone independently arrives at an identical world. Bandwidth is a few hundred bytes a second regardless of what is happening on screen.

Verified here: two processes played the same match and logged byte-identical checksums at every one of 480 ticks.

See MULTIPLAYER.md for internet play and known limitations.

body:
First build with audio. Linux and Windows, same commit.

## Run it

**Linux**
```
unzip shoosting-linux64.zip -d shoosting && cd shoosting
chmod +x shoosting && ./shoosting
```

**Windows** — unzip and run `shoosting.exe`. Mono backend, since IL2CPP cannot cross-compile from Linux; fine for playtesting, and determinism is unaffected because the simulation is integer-only fixed point.

Flags: `-skipmenu` drops straight into a match, `-stage 1` loads THE LANES instead of BRANDEE.

## Controls

WASD move, **Space** jump, mouse aim, **LMB** fire, **RMB** block, **Shift** dash, **Esc** menu.
Player 2 shares the keyboard: arrows move, IJKL aim, RShift fire, `/` block, RCtrl dash, RAlt jump.

## What to listen for

Sounds are synthesised in code as placeholders, so judge the *behaviour* rather than the fidelity:

- **Wall grabs** — climb an outer pillar. Should be a rhythm of soft falling tones, one per grab, not a stutter.
- **Skids** — reverse direction at speed on the ground. Pitch and volume scale with how much speed the turn is fighting, so a gentle scrub and a hard reversal should sound clearly different. This is the momentum model made audible.
- **Block** (RMB) — deflects a shot back at whoever fired it, on a 5s cooldown. The ring shows state: bright = active, dim = recovering, absent = ready.

Nobody has actually heard any of this. There is no audio device on the build machine, so the balance between sounds is an untested first guess — if one drowns the others, that is the most likely fault.

body:
It is a run now, not a deathmatch.

## What is new

**Bots.** Player 1 is a bot by default. `-difficulty rookie|regular|sharp|brutal`, `-bots 0` for two-keyboard hotseat, `-bots 2` for an all-bot match that plays itself.

Difficulty is **reaction delay and aim error only** — never extra health or damage. Rookie reacts in half a second and never lands a block; Brutal reacts in under a tenth and blocks constantly.

**Cards.** After each round the **loser** picks one of three. Twelve to start:

Bullet Time · Buckshot · Bouncy · Overcharge · Feather · Double Jump · Dasher · Gecko · Parry · Vampire · Glass · Grenadier

The winner never picks, even when behind on the match score — winning a round is its own reward. The interesting cards carry a cost: Overcharge trades recoil for damage, Glass trades fragility for damage, Grenadier trades a flat trajectory for explosions.

## Run it

**Linux** — `unzip shoosting-linux64.zip -d shoosting && cd shoosting && chmod +x shoosting && ./shoosting`
**Windows** — unzip, run `shoosting.exe`

## Worth trying

- Lose a few rounds on purpose and watch the escalation. Grenadier plus Bouncy is chaos.
- Fight a Brutal bot and try to bait its block, then punish the 5s cooldown.
- `-bots 2 -difficulty brutal` and just watch two bots escalate against each other.

Sounds are still code-synthesised placeholders.
